issues.legal_issue: A landlord may obtain possession of non-residential premises for a partnership business when the evidence establishes the landlord’s bona fide requirement and the intended work is part of, or allied to, the partnership’s existing business.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession for a partnership that dealt in paper, paper products, and stationery.
The partnership also carried out cutting, printing, and binding through job workers, and intended to undertake that work in the premises.

A witness holding the landlord’s power of attorney testified to the partnership’s need and produced documents showing its work; the witness’s knowledge of the business was not challenged in cross-examination.
The lower authorities and the High Court considered the landlord’s requirement and sustained the order on the ground of bona fide requirement.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the order for possession, finding evidence of the landlord’s requirement and that the intended work was allied to the partnership’s existing business, not an entirely new business.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 permits a landlord to seek possession of a qualifying non-residential building when the landlord is not occupying a qualifying building of the landlord’s own for a business carried on by the landlord. The landlord’s requirement is relevant to the inquiry, as reflected in S. Peer Mohammed v. B. Mohan Lal Sowcar. On the evidence here, work involving cutting, printing, and binding was allied to dealing in paper and paper products.

predicates.appeal_against_business_premises_evictio: The matter is an appeal concerning an order requiring a tenant to give up business premises.
predicates.landlord_seeks_premises_for_partnership_: The landlord seeks the premises for use in a partnership business.
predicates.evidence_supports_landlord_requirement: Testimony or other evidence supports the landlord’s stated requirement, and the evidence is not undermined on the record.
predicates.intended_work_is_allied_to_existing_busi: The work intended for the premises is part of or allied to the partnership’s existing business.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns eviction from business premises sought for a partnership, evidence supports the landlord’s requirement, and the intended work is allied to the existing business, the eviction order is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A sleeping-partner objection to recovery of premises for a partnership business cannot be considered when its factual foundation was not pleaded or established in the record.
material_facts: The tenant argued in the Supreme Court that the landlord was merely a sleeping partner and could not recover the premises for the partnership’s business.
The argument had not been raised earlier and was not included in the tenant’s written statement.

The partnership deed assigned management and day-to-day affairs to the other partner, but also contained a clause requiring a partner to attend diligently to the partnership business for the partners’ greatest advantage.
The record did not establish that the landlord was a mere sleeping partner.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the sleeping-partner argument because its factual foundation had not been laid in the written statement or established by the record.
issues.legal_principle: D.N. Sanghvi and Sons v. Ambalal Tribhuwan Das and Krishnan Nair v. Ghouse Basha were cited for the principle that a sleeping partner is not entitled to recover premises he owns for the purposes of the partnership business. The Court did not decide the argument on its merits: it held that the necessary factual foundation should have been pleaded so that evidence could be led. Its assumption that a new point of law might be raised where that foundation exists was not a determination of that question.
